0: Map every request from browser to frontend, API, database, and back before adding abstractions.
Keep presentation, business rules, and persistence responsibilities intentionally separated.
Treat TaskFlow as one continuous system so each phase extends an architecture you already understand.
Use version locks as a reproducibility contract, not as a reason to ignore underlying concepts.
1: Verify tools from the terminal instead of assuming an installer succeeded.
Understand PATH, ports, processes, shells, and working directories because they explain many setup failures.
Prefer user-level development tooling when administrator privileges are unnecessary.
Record exact versions and verification commands so another developer can reproduce the environment.
2: A monorepo should make shared ownership and coordinated changes easier, not merely put folders in one repository.
Use pnpm workspaces to make package boundaries explicit and dependency installation deterministic.
Keep shared configuration in dedicated packages instead of duplicating compiler and lint settings.
Run repository-wide tasks from the root while allowing app-specific commands when debugging.
3: Use Server Components by default and introduce Client Components only where browser interactivity requires them.
Treat the App Router file system as application structure, not as a place to hide business rules.
Keep secrets and privileged data access on the server side of the Next.js boundary.
Understand caching and rendering behavior before trying to fix stale UI with ad-hoc client state.
4: Controllers translate HTTP concerns; services own application behavior and orchestration.
Dependency injection makes dependencies explicit and replaceable instead of hiding them in global imports.
Use Fastify as the HTTP adapter without leaking adapter-specific details through the entire application.
Organize NestJS modules around cohesive features rather than one giant application module.
5: Design APIs around resources, contracts, and HTTP semantics rather than controller method names.
Use status codes consistently so clients can distinguish validation, authentication, authorization, and missing resources.
Make request and response contracts explicit enough that frontend and backend can evolve safely.
Treat idempotency, pagination, errors, and concurrency as API design concerns, not afterthoughts.
6: Keep the browser dependent on a stable API contract rather than importing backend implementation details.
Configure CORS narrowly for the origins that should call the API.
Centralize base URLs and environment-specific configuration instead of hard-coding localhost throughout components.
Trace failures across browser network tools, API logs, and server responses rather than guessing from UI symptoms.
7: Model data around entities, relationships, constraints, and access patterns before writing application queries.
Use transactions when multiple writes must succeed or fail as one unit.
Add indexes to support real query patterns, not every column indiscriminately.
Let database constraints defend invariants that must remain true regardless of application code.
8: Treat Supabase Postgres as PostgreSQL first; managed services do not remove relational design responsibilities.
Separate connection details, credentials, and environment configuration from source code.
Understand pooling and connection limits before scaling application instances.
Use the Supabase dashboard as an operational tool, not as a substitute for migrations and repeatable schema changes.
9: Use Prisma migrations as the authoritative history of application schema changes.
Keep generated Prisma Client code derived from the schema instead of hand-editing it.
Use a shared Prisma service in NestJS so connection lifecycle and access patterns remain controlled.
Pin Prisma versions deliberately when the course architecture depends on a specific configuration model.
10: Normalize relationships enough to preserve correctness before optimizing for convenience.
Choose cardinality intentionally: one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many model different business rules.
Use unique constraints and foreign keys to encode invariants where the database can enforce them.
Design TaskFlow entities around actual workflows such as workspaces, members, boards, lists, tasks, comments, and labels.
11: CRUD endpoints are complete only when data persists and failure cases are handled deliberately.
Keep database calls behind service methods so controllers remain thin and testable.
Return the created or updated resource contract consistently after successful mutations.
Verify persistence independently with API requests and database inspection instead of trusting only the UI.
12: Validate external input at the application boundary before business logic trusts it.
Use schemas to produce both runtime checks and reusable TypeScript types where appropriate.
Distinguish transport validation from domain/business rules because they fail for different reasons.
Return validation errors that help clients correct input without exposing internal implementation details.
13: Map known failures to stable HTTP error responses instead of leaking raw exceptions.
Keep unexpected errors observable to operators while returning safe messages to clients.
Use consistent error shapes so frontend code does not branch on dozens of unrelated formats.
Preserve enough context in logs to diagnose an error without sending secrets to the browser.
14: Business rules belong in services or domain-focused collaborators, not duplicated across controllers and components.
Keep orchestration separate from low-level persistence details so behavior can be tested clearly.
Make rule boundaries explicit before adding abstractions such as repositories.
Prefer small cohesive methods that communicate intent over giant service methods that mix validation, authorization, and I/O.
15: Filtering, sorting, and pagination must use deterministic query rules so results remain stable.
Validate user-supplied sort fields instead of injecting arbitrary column names into queries.
Pagination metadata should match the strategy used by the API so clients can navigate correctly.
Indexes should follow real filter and sort patterns when performance data shows they are needed.
16: Authentication establishes who a caller is; authorization decides what that identity may do.
Passwords, sessions, tokens, and cookies solve different parts of identity management and have different risks.
Treat credentials and tokens as secrets in transit, storage, logs, and browser code.
Design authentication flows around expiration, revocation, renewal, and failure states rather than only the happy path.
17: Let Supabase Auth establish user identity while the application still owns TaskFlow authorization rules.
Keep service-role credentials off the browser and use public client credentials only for intended client operations.
Handle session restoration and expiration explicitly so UI state does not silently drift from server identity.
Verify authentication on the server for protected operations rather than trusting client-visible session state.
18: NestJS guards should verify identity before protected controllers execute.
Derive the authenticated user from a verified token, never from a user id supplied by the browser.
Attach validated identity to the request in one controlled place so downstream code can consume it consistently.
Return 401 for missing or invalid authentication and reserve 403 for authenticated callers lacking permission.
19: Enforce ownership and role checks on the server even when the UI hides forbidden actions.
Model permissions around actions and resources instead of scattering role-name comparisons everywhere.
Check workspace membership before allowing resource operations tied to that workspace.
Use least privilege: a role should receive only the capabilities its workflows require.
20: Build production UI from reusable layout and interaction patterns, not a collection of one-off pages.
Represent loading, empty, error, success, and permission states explicitly.
Accessibility and responsive behavior are requirements of the component, not a final polishing step.
Keep UI composition separate from server-state ownership so components remain understandable.
21: React Hook Form should own transient form interaction while Zod defines the input contract.
Validate close to the user for feedback, but repeat trust-boundary validation on the backend.
Map server validation errors back to fields without losing non-field errors.
Reset or preserve form state deliberately after successful mutations based on the workflow.
22: TanStack Query owns asynchronous server state; it is not a replacement for every kind of React state.
Choose query keys that uniquely describe the data and parameters being cached.
Invalidate or update the relevant cache after mutations so UI state converges with the server.
Configure stale time and refetch behavior based on data freshness needs rather than copying defaults blindly.
23: Put shareable navigation state in the URL, server state in TanStack Query, and local interaction state near the component that owns it.
Avoid duplicating the same piece of state across URL, React state, and query cache.
Derive values when possible instead of synchronizing multiple mutable copies.
Choose state ownership by lifecycle and source of truth, not by whichever library is fashionable.
24: Introduce a repository only when separating persistence behavior creates a real testing or architecture benefit.
A repository should express persistence operations in application terms rather than mirror every ORM method.
Keep Prisma-specific details from leaking through layers if the repository is intended to create a meaningful boundary.
Do not add repository abstractions to trivial CRUD solely because the pattern exists.
25: Optimistic updates must define how to snapshot, apply, roll back, and reconcile state.
Use optimism where failure is uncommon and the user benefit justifies rollback complexity.
Handle concurrent mutations and stale responses so an older result cannot overwrite newer user intent.
Always reconcile optimistic client state with authoritative server state.
26: Realtime is a synchronization mechanism, not the authoritative database.
Subscribe only to events relevant to the current user and resource scope.
Design reconnect and duplicate-event behavior so clients can recover after temporary disconnection.
Reconcile realtime events with cached server state rather than maintaining an unrelated second data model.
27: Keep file bytes in object storage and metadata/authorization relationships in application data where appropriate.
Validate file type, size, path, and ownership before trusting an upload workflow.
Use signed or access-controlled URLs instead of making private files globally public.
Treat deletion as a coordinated workflow when both storage objects and database metadata must remain consistent.
28: Use unit tests for focused behavior, integration tests for collaborating infrastructure, and end-to-end tests for critical user flows.
Test business outcomes and contracts rather than coupling every test to private implementation details.
Keep tests deterministic by controlling clocks, random values, external services, and database state where necessary.
A useful test suite catches regressions while remaining fast enough to run continuously in development and CI.
29: Threat-model trust boundaries before applying random security checklists.
Validate and authorize every sensitive server operation even if the frontend already restricts the UI.
Keep secrets out of source control, client bundles, logs, and error responses.
Use layered defenses for common web risks such as injection, broken access control, unsafe uploads, and misconfiguration.
30: Logs should answer what happened, where, and for which request without exposing sensitive data.
Use request or correlation identifiers to connect events across application boundaries.
Metrics reveal system trends while traces and structured logs help explain individual failures.
Alert on user-impacting symptoms and actionable conditions rather than every noisy internal event.
31: Measure before optimizing so work targets real bottlenecks instead of intuition.
Reduce unnecessary network requests, database queries, rendering work, and payload size before reaching for exotic caching.
Use indexes and query plans when database latency is the bottleneck.
Performance work must preserve correctness, observability, and maintainability.
32: A Dockerfile should produce a repeatable image from declared inputs rather than depend on a developer machine.
Use multi-stage builds to keep runtime images smaller and separate build-time tools from production dependencies.
Do not bake secrets into images; inject runtime configuration through the deployment environment.
Health checks and graceful shutdown help orchestrators know when a container is ready and when it should be replaced.
33: CI verifies changes on pull requests; release workflows should operate from trusted code and immutable commit identities.
Use frozen lockfile installs so CI fails when dependency manifests and the lockfile disagree.
Give GitHub Actions tokens the minimum permissions each job requires.
Build once and promote the same artifact instead of rebuilding different binaries for each environment.
34: Production deployment is a system of frontend, API, database, DNS, secrets, migrations, and observability rather than one deploy button.
Apply database migrations in a controlled step before code depends on the new schema.
Use environment-specific configuration while keeping the same tested application artifact where possible.
Plan smoke tests and rollback before release so recovery is part of deployment design.
35: Refactoring should improve boundaries and clarity while preserving externally observable behavior.
Use tests and architecture checks as safety nets before moving responsibilities across modules.
Remove abstractions that no longer earn their complexity instead of only adding new layers.
Document significant architectural decisions so future maintainers understand the trade-offs that shaped the system.
36: Enterprise scaling starts by identifying new business boundaries, compliance needs, load, and organizational ownership.
Keep the modular monolith viable until scale or team boundaries justify distributing the system.
Add queues, caches, services, and orchestration only for concrete bottlenecks or ownership needs.
Design replaceable infrastructure interfaces so managed services can evolve without rewriting core business rules.
